reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: A rare congenital malformation in which the aortic valve has four cusps instead of the normal three
Cusps are classified by their relative sizes, with configurations ranging from four equal cusps to one with three equal and one smaller cusp
Aortic regurgitation is the dominant functional lesion, usually developing gradually because the asymmetric cusps coapt imperfectly
Many patients are asymptomatic in early life and are diagnosed incidentally on echocardiography or at surgery
Progressive regurgitation can cause left ventricular volume loading, dilatation and eventual symptoms of heart failure
Associated anomalies include coronary artery ostial displacement, which is relevant if surgery is planned
Management follows aortic valve disease principles, with surveillance of regurgitation severity and valve repair or replacement when indicated
reference.pathophysiology: A quadricuspid aortic valve arises from abnormal septation of the truncal cushions during valvulogenesis, producing four cusps rather than three. The supernumerary and often unequally sized cusps close incompletely, so the valve tends towards regurgitation over time as repeated imperfect coaptation causes cusp fibrosis and prolapse. The resulting chronic aortic regurgitation imposes a volume load on the left ventricle, which dilates and hypertrophies to compensate before contractile function eventually declines. Stenosis is much less common. Because the abnormal cusp arrangement can be associated with displacement of the coronary ostia, coronary anatomy is an important consideration when intervention is contemplated.
additionalDifferentials: Tricuspid aortic valve with degenerative regurgitation
Infective endocarditis of the aortic valve
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to count cusps and grade regurgitation
Transoesophageal echocardiography for detailed cusp morphology when transthoracic views are limited
Cardiac MRI to quantify regurgitant volume and left ventricular size and function
Cardiac CT to assess valve anatomy and coronary ostial position before surgery
Serial imaging to monitor progression of regurgitation and ventricular remodelling
redFlags: Severe aortic regurgitation with progressive left ventricular dilatation or dysfunction
New symptoms of heart failure or exertional intolerance
Superimposed infective endocarditis on the abnormal valve
Displaced coronary ostia complicating planned intervention
reference.prognosis: Many patients remain well for decades, but a substantial proportion develop significant aortic regurgitation requiring valve surgery in adulthood; outcomes after timely repair or replacement are generally good.
pitfalls: Miscounting cusps and mistaking the valve for a bicuspid or tricuspid valve on limited imaging
Underestimating slowly progressive regurgitation and delaying surveillance
Overlooking coronary ostial anomalies before surgery
Attributing regurgitation solely to root dilatation without recognising the cusp anomaly
